title: International Convention on Civil Liability for Oil Pollution Damage

{{Short description|1969 international maritime treaty}}
{{EngvarB|date=May 2013}}

{{Admiralty law}}

The '''International Convention on Civil Liability for Oil Pollution Damage, 1969''', renewed in 1992 and often referred to as the '''CLC Convention''', is an international maritime treaty administered by the [[International Maritime Organization]] that was adopted to ensure that adequate compensation would be available where oil pollution damage was caused by maritime casualties involving [[oil tankers]] (i.e. ships that carry oil as cargo).<ref name="imo.org">International Maritime Organization on the International Convention on Civil Liability for Oil Pollution Damage (CLC), 1969 [http://www.imo.org/About/Conventions/ListOfConventions/Pages/International-Convention-on-Civil-Liability-for-Oil-Pollution-Damage-(CLC).aspx] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120316005034/http://www.imo.org/About/Conventions/ListOfConventions/Pages/International-Convention-on-Civil-Liability-for-Oil-Pollution-Damage-(CLC).aspx |date=16 March 2012 }}</ref>

== Liability ==
The convention introduces [[strict liability]] for shipowners.<ref>R. Bhanu Krishna Kiran, [http://nujslawreview.org/2016/12/03/liability-and-compensation-for-oil-pollution-damage-an-examination-of-imo-conventions/ "Liability and Compensation for Oil Pollution Damage: An examination of IMO Convention"], ''NUJS LAW REVIEW'', 2 January 2015, Accessed on 1 July 2017</ref>

In cases when the shipowner is deemed guilty of fault for an instance of oil pollution, the convention does not cap liability.

When the shipowner is not at fault, the convention caps liability at between 3 million [[special drawing rights]] (SDR) for a ship of {{GT|5,000}} to 59.7 million SDR for ships over {{GT|140,000}}.

The 2000 Amendments

Adoption: 18 October 2000

Entry into force: 1 November 2003

The amendments raised the compensation limits by 50 percent compared to the limits set in the 1992 Protocol, as follows:  
For a ship not exceeding 5,000 gross tonnage, liability is limited to 4.51 million SDR (US$5.78 million)
For a ship 5,000 to 140,000 gross tonnage:  liability is limited to 4.51 million SDR plus 631 SDR for each additional gross tonne over 5,000
For a ship over 140,000 gross tonnage: liability is limited to 89.77 million SDR

The [[HNS Convention]] to compensation for damages occurring from spill of [[dangerous goods]] is based on the same legal framework.<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.hnsconvention.org/Pages/TheConvention.aspx|title=HNS Convention Legal Framework|access-date=2014-02-13|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140201225527/http://www.hnsconvention.org/Pages/TheConvention.aspx|archive-date=1 February 2014}}</ref>

== Insurance ==

If a ship carries more than 2000 tons of oil in cargo, CLC requires shipowners to maintain "insurance or other financial security" sufficient to cover the maximum liability for one oil spill<ref name="imo.org"/>

== Coverage ==
As of September 2016, 136 states, representing 97.5 per cent of the world fleet, are contracting parties to the '''CLC Protocol''' of 1992, which amends the original CLC Convention.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.imo.org/About/Conventions/StatusOfConventions/Pages/Default.aspx |title=International Maritime Organization – Status of Conventions |access-date=21 March 2012 |archive-date=15 April 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120415174106/http://www.imo.org/About/Conventions/StatusOfConventions/Pages/Default.aspx |url-status=dead }}</ref> [[Bolivia]], [[North Korea]], [[Honduras]], and [[Lebanon]]—which are generally [[flag of convenience]] states—have not ratified the treaty.<ref name="marisec">{{cite book |title=Shipping Industry Flag State Performance Table |last=MARISEC |year=2009 |publisher=Maritime International Secretariat Services |location=London |pages=1–2 |url=http://www.marisec.org/shippingfacts/uploads/File/FlagStatePerformanceTable09.pdf?SID=lghwfzybi |access-date=2010-06-12}}{{dead link|date=February 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

The [[United States of America]] is not a signatory to CLC, despite considerable involvement in its formulation. This is due to significant nation legislation such as the [[Oil Pollution Act, 1990]], so signing the CLC was deemed unnecessary.<ref>{{cite web|title=LIABILITY AND COMPENSATION FOR SHIP-SOURCE OIL POLLUTION|url=http://unctad.org/en/PublicationsLibrary/dtltlb20114_en.pdf|website=unctad.org|publisher=United Nations Conference on Trade and Development|access-date=30 June 2017|pages=20, 23|date=31 January 2012|quote=[p20:] in some cases, substantial compensation may be available under applicable national law, as for instance in the case of the United States Oil Pollution Act 1990 (OPA 1990). [and p23:] [Non-signatories] includes notably the United States, where, however, strong national legislation to provide for liability and compensation has been enacted.}}</ref>
